Like, the teacher would explain an assignment, and by step two, my brain was just somewhere else entirely and I'd have to ask what we were supposed to do again. And group work! Oh my gosh, group work was probably a nightmare for my friends because I would just talk right over my classmates. I’d get so excited about an idea, or I'd just get impatient with how slow someone else was explaining something, and I’d just blurt things out. I really wasn't trying to be rude or bossy, I just... It's a really amazing tool, but it's also kind of a trap for me. Because what happens is, someone in my group will be explaining their concept, right? Like they're maybe halfway through talking about how they want the user flow to work or explaining their color palette, and my brain will just make a connection and I'll get this massive flash of an idea. \n\nAnd instead of just holding onto it and waiting for them to finish their sentence like a normal person, I'll just completely blurt it out. I'll just talk right over them. Or, honestly, sometimes even worse, I won't even say anything at all, I'll just start physically adding things to their Figma board while they're still talking. Yeah, unfortunately, it really does. It's actually been causing me a lot of stress lately, to be completely honest. Because, well, I don't have a formal job right now since I'm a full-time student, but I try to take on these small freelance design contracts when I can, just to build up my resume and make a little extra money. But I've actually lost a couple of them recently. There was this one just a few months ago where I was supposed to design some branding assets for a local indie coffee shop, and I had all these amazing concepts—like, I spent hours sketching out these really cool, intricate cup designs—but I just couldn't pull the final deliverables together cleanly. I missed the deadline for the second round of revisions because I got completely sidetracked trying to reinvent a logo they had already approved, and eventually the owner just had to pull the plug. He was nice about it, but he basically said they couldn't rely on me to just follow through on the actual timeline, which was so embarrassing.

And it totally affects my school stuff, too. Like, I completely missed out on this huge departmental portfolio competition last semester. The deadline was marked on my calendar, I had reminders set, but I just kept endlessly tweaking the layout of my pages instead of actually finalizing the files. And then I didn't read the submission guidelines closely enough, so I missed that we were supposed to include this specific artist statement, and by the time I realized it and tried to scramble to write one, the online portal had already closed. It was just... ugh, it was devastating because I really wanted to participate and I knew my work was good enough, but I just couldn't get it together to actually submit it properly. 

And then with relationships... I mean, my friends are amazing, but I can definitely tell my behavior takes a toll on them. Like I was saying earlier about the Figma boards and talking over people? It's gotten to the point where some of my friends and the people I usually collaborate with in my cohort are actually hesitant to work with me now. Which really, really hurts. They'll tell me they love my ideas and that I bring a lot of creative energy to the table, but when it comes time to pick partners for a major semester-long project, I can see them kind of avoiding my eye. They just know that I'm going to be chaotic to manage and that I might drop the ball on the organizational parts of the project. It just feels awful knowing people think you're unreliable, even when you're trying so incredibly hard to keep everything on track, you know? It just feels like I'm constantly getting in my own way.

Oh, completely. It's actually one of the things that frustrates me the most about myself, because I really do care about the quality of my work, I promise I do, but the details just... they just slip right past me, no matter how hard I try to catch them. 

Like, I'll spend hours and hours on a project, right? And in that moment, I'm sitting there thinking, "Wow, this is perfect, this is so polished, they're going to absolutely love it." I feel so proud of it. 

And then, inevitably, I'll look at the file again the next morning, or worse, the professor or the client will email me back with feedback, and I'll realize I did something so incredibly careless. Like, I'll look at the data chart and realize I completely mislabeled an X or Y axis. Or I'll be looking at a design mockup and see that I used the completely wrong color key—like, maybe their brand guidelines specifically said to use this exact hex code for their secondary blue, and I just totally glossed over it and used the default blue from my swatches panel instead because I was moving too fast. 

Or, and this happens a lot, I'll realize I just completely missed a tiny instruction in the client brief. Like, they'll have this one little bullet point buried in paragraph three that says, I don't know, "make sure the logo is always bottom-left," and I'll have put it on the top-right because I thought it balanced the page better visually, completely forgetting that they explicitly asked for something else. 

And it's just so embarrassing! Because it makes it look like I didn't care enough to read the instructions or double-check my work, but I *did* check it! I swear I checked it before I submitted it. It's just that my brain... it literally just does not see the mistake. It's like I have a total blind spot for the tiny, technical things once I get hyper-focused on the big picture and the creative side of it. And it just ruins all the hard work I put into the rest of the design, you know? Because people don't see the hours you spent on the concept, they just see that you spelled "company" wrong or messed up a chart, and then they think you're sloppy. It just drives me crazy because I know I'm smart enough to catch these things, but I just... don't.

Like, I wasn't struggling to grasp the concepts, I just literally could not force my brain to stay on the path from start to finish without someone holding my hand and redirecting me every two minutes. They literally had to take turns sitting right beside me at the kitchen table every single night just to make sure I actually did it. It was just so frustrating for them, I think, because they knew I understood the material, you know? I'll constantly be shifting my weight or bouncing my leg or fiddling with my rings just to relieve that weird tension. My parents had to literally sit right next to me at the kitchen table every single night to get me to do my homework. If they got up to stir a pot on the stove or answer the phone, I was gone. I'd wander off into the living room, or I'd start, I don't know, trying to build a tower out of my erasers instead of finishing my math problems. They had to be there to physically keep me on task. There was this one boy in my third-grade class, Jason, who literally could not stay in his chair. He was always getting up to sharpen his pencil, or look out the window, or just kind of wander over to the reading corner, and the teacher was constantly telling him to sit back down. But I don't think I ever did that. I mean, I was definitely squirmy in my seat, you know? Like, I'd cross and uncross my legs a million times, or I'd lean all the way back until the front legs of the chair came off the floor—which, actually, I did fall backward once in fifth grade and it made this huge crash and everyone stared at me, which was mortifying. But I wasn't actually getting up and walking around the room. \n\nI think I was too worried about getting in trouble to actually leave my desk. I was a bit of a rule-follower when it came to the big, obvious rules like \"stay in your seat.\" My way of, I guess, being restless was more about fidgeting with my hands under the desk, or doodling all over the margins of my notebooks, or just completely zoning out and staring at the clock. But physically getting up and leaving my seat during a lesson or when we were supposed to be working? No, I really don't think I did that. Even at home, when I was doing homework, I might have gotten distracted and started playing with my erasers, like I said before, but I was still sitting at the kitchen table. So, yeah, I'd have to say no to that one. I don't remember that being a problem for me before I was twelve. Or ever, really.\n\nDoctor: Before age 12, were you often fidgety or unable to stay seated in class?\n\nPatient: Wait, didn't you just ask me that? Or... wait, no, you asked about *leaving* my seat. Okay, sorry, my brain is just kind of spinning right now. But fidgety? Oh my gosh, yes. Yes, absolutely. I mean, I just mentioned the chair leaning thing, but it's so much more than that, and honestly, it hasn't changed at all since I was a kid. \n\nLike, even now, in college—I'm a sophomore, by the way—when I'm in my studio classes or, God forbid, a portfolio review where I actually have to sit still and listen to the professors critique my work? I am constantly moving. It's like I have this nervous energy that just has to go somewhere. I'll be sitting there, and I don't even realize I'm doing it, but my leg will be bouncing up and down like a jackhammer. Or I'll have a pen in my hand, and I'll just be clicking it, click-click-click-click, until the person next to me gives me this death glare. \n\nAnd if I don't have a pen, I'm twisting my rings around my fingers, taking them off, putting them back on, switching them to different fingers. Or I'm just constantly shifting my weight in the chair, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, tucking one foot under me, then the other. It's like no position is ever comfortable for more than two minutes. And the worst part is, I usually have no idea I'm even doing it until someone actually looks at me or says something. It's completely unconscious. It's just... it's like my body refuses to just exist quietly. So, yeah, the fidgeting is definitely a huge thing, and it's always been there, way before I was twelve, and it's still happening right now. Like, I'm literally twisting my ring right now as I'm talking to you.\n\nDoctor: Before age 12, did you often have trouble waiting your turn?\n\nPatient: Oh, waiting my turn? Yeah. Yes, definitely before twelve, just like the other things. But honestly, it's one of those things that has just never, ever gone away, so it's almost easier to think about how bad it is right now, because it's the exact same feeling I had when I was a kid waiting for the swings at recess. \n\nLike, I do a lot of UI/UX design, so I go to these weekend hackathons with the computer science kids, right? And the check-in lines on Friday nights are just... they are agonizing. I get really, really antsy waiting for my turn to just get my lanyard and get inside. I'll be standing there, and I catch myself constantly checking the time on my phone, like every thirty seconds, shifting my weight around, looking to see if the other lines are moving faster. It feels like my skin is crawling just from having to stand there and do nothing while other people take their time.\n\nAnd it happens during office-hour queues, too. That might actually be worse. If I need help with a portfolio piece and there are, like, three people ahead of me waiting to talk to the professor, I am just a total mess out in the hallway. I get this overwhelming urge to just jump in before it’s actually my turn. I'll hear the person inside asking a question, and I'll think, \"Oh my gosh, they are taking forever, let me just pop in and get my quick question answered,\" and I have to physically stop myself from barging through the door. I just want to jump in and get it over with. It's just this intense, physical impatience. I hate the feeling of being stalled or held up by other people's pacing. So, yeah, it definitely started when I was little, but it's still a massive issue for me literally every time I have to stand in a line."
